title: Factorising Algebraic Expressions
subject: Mathematics
subtopic: Common factors, difference of squares and trinomials

scenes.heading: Factorising
scenes.narration: Welcome to part two of our Grade 9 algebra series. In this lesson we factorise expressions using a common factor, the difference of two squares, and trinomials.

scenes.heading: What is factorising?
bullets: Factorising is the opposite of expanding
We write an expression as a product of factors
Always look for a common factor first
scenes.narration: Factorising is the opposite of expanding. Instead of multiplying out brackets, we put them back, writing the expression as a product of factors. The golden rule: always look for a common factor first.

scenes.heading: Common factor
scenes.narration: Factorise six x squared plus nine x. The highest common factor of six and nine is three, and both terms have an x, so the common factor is three x. Six x squared divided by three x is two x. Nine x divided by three x is three. So the answer is three x times, two x plus three.

scenes.heading: Difference of two squares
scenes.narration: A difference of two squares, a squared minus b squared, factorises to a minus b, times a plus b. So x squared minus forty nine is x minus seven, times x plus seven. And four y squared minus twenty five: four y squared is two y all squared, and twenty five is five squared. So it is two y minus five, times two y plus five.

scenes.heading: Trinomials
scenes.narration: Factorise x squared, plus seven x, plus twelve. Find two numbers that multiply to give twelve, and add to give seven. Three and four work: three times four is twelve, and three plus four is seven. So the answer is x plus three, times x plus four.

scenes.heading: Trinomial with negatives
scenes.narration: Factorise x squared, minus two x, minus fifteen. We need two numbers with a product of negative fifteen and a sum of negative two. Negative five and three work: negative five times three is negative fifteen, and negative five plus three is negative two. So the answer is x minus five, times x plus three.

scenes.heading: Common factor first
scenes.narration: Factorise two x squared minus eighteen. Eighteen is not a perfect square, but take out the common factor two first. That leaves x squared minus nine, which is a difference of two squares. So the answer is two, times x minus three, times x plus three.

scenes.heading: Tips
bullets: Common factor first, then look for other types
Two terms with a minus between squares: difference of two squares
Check your answer by expanding it
scenes.narration: To sum up: always take out a common factor first. If there are two perfect squares with a minus between them, use the difference of two squares. For a trinomial, find two numbers for the product and the sum. And check your answer by expanding it.
